aesthete: Aesthete sounds like “S-thete”: someone who is “thete” about beauty, standing for hours in front of a painting.
The friend who rearranges your flowers and sighs at an ugly font: lives for beauty.
aesthetic: Greek aisthesis = perception by the senses. Aesthetics is what looks, sounds and feels good.
An-aesthetic removes feeling; aesthetic is the feeling of beauty. Remove the “an”.
apathetic: A + pathos: no passion. The student who shrugs: “Whatever.”
Apathy sounds like “a path-y”: someone who won’t walk any path because they don’t care where it goes.
audacious: Aud: audio + dare (audere): speaks loudly and dares. An audacious plan: dare to try it.
Think of Danton’s « De l’audace ! »: boldness, for good or bad.
banal: Banal comes from feudal ban: things everyone in the village shared, so common to all. Hence ordinary.
Elevator music: heard so much it’s lost its flavour. Banal.
bucolic: Bou- = cow (Greek bous). Bucolic scene: cows and a meadow, peaceful countryside.
Think “bucket-olic”: a milk bucket in the pasture. Idyllic rural life.
chortle: Lewis Carroll invented it: chuckle + snort. He wrote “he chortled in his joy” in Jabberwocky.
Chortle sounds like a throaty giggle: a snorting laugh after a clever pun.
concede: Con + cedere (yield): hand over the point. Concede defeat after the election.
Cédez le passage: you give way to the other. To concede = to give way.
conspicuous: Con + specere (to look): easy to see from afar. A pink coat in a grey crowd.
Conspicuous = you can’t miss it. A neon sign in a dark street.
cryptic: Crypt = hidden chamber. A cryptic crossword clue hides its answer underground.
A text from your boss: “We need to talk.” Cryptic: no explanation.
culminate: Culmen = summit. A mountain climb culminates at the peak.
Think “culminating” = reaching the culmination, the top of the staircase.
culpability: Culpa: mea culpa, “my fault”. Culpability = how much blame is yours.
Culprit and culpable share the root: the one guilty of the act.
decorous: Decor-ous: acts in keeping with the decor of the occasion: a funeral calls for a quiet voice.
Décorum: dressing and behaving as the setting demands. Decorous = proper.
deferential: De + ferre (carry): you carry your opinion down to let the other’s win. Bow to authority.
Par déférence: a junior who lets the senior speak first.
dictatorial: Dictate + oral: someone who orders everyone else around like a dictator.
In a dictatorial office, the boss decides everything and employees only take notes.
didactic: Didaskein = to teach. A didactic poem is a lecture in verse. A little preachy.
Didactic = “die-dactic”: the teacher who talks until the class dies of boredom.
diffident: Dis + fidere (trust): lack of trust in oneself. A shy speaker who whispers.
Diffident ≈ « défiant » but turned inward: you don’t trust your own voice.
dogmatic: Dog + matic: a bulldog that won’t let go of its opinion. Rigid belief.
Dogma = official doctrine. A dogmatic debater cites it and refuses discussion.
engender: En + gender: to give birth to something, like a cause bringing about an effect. Engendrer.
“Engender” has gen = birth (generate, genesis). Hate engenders violence.
entrenched: Trench warfare: dug in and unlikely to move. An entrenched habit.
A tree with deep roots: entrenched, almost impossible to remove.
eschew: Say “es-chew”: you chew and spit out the thing you refuse. Avoid on purpose.
Esquiver: dodge. Eschew sugar = avoid it by choice.
exacerbate: Ex + acerbus (bitter): make more bitter. Rubbing salt in a wound.
Acerbic = sharp. To exacerbate = to make the pain sharper.
fortuitous: Fortuit: by chance, not planned. It doesn’t mean fortunate: just a lucky or unlucky accident.
Fortuitous sounds like “fortune”, but think “random fortune”: a coin falling just so.
frivolous: Frivole: light as a feather, not serious. A frivolous lawsuit over a spilled coffee.
Frivolous = “free of weight”: it floats away because it has no substance.
gainsay: Gain = against (as in again-st). Gainsay = say against: contradict.
“Who can gainsay the evidence?” No one can deny it.
gall: Gall bladder = bile = bitterness. To have the gall = the bitter nerve to do something rude.
Avoir le culot: gall has the cheek of someone who asks for the boss’s job on day one.
germane: Germane ≈ germain: cousins-german are close cousins. A germane remark is closely related.
Related like a sibling: germane points belong in the discussion.
glut: Glutton: the market is so full that it can’t eat any more. Too much supply.
Un trop-plein: a glut of grapes means a price crash.
gossamer: Goose + summer: the thin silk that floats in the air on warm autumn days. Very light cloth.
Gossamer wings of a dragonfly: you see through them, they weigh nothing.
impudent: Im + pudent (pudeur, shame): has no shame. A kid sticking out his tongue at the teacher.
Impudent = no pudeur: the child who walks into your meeting and tells the boss he’s wrong. Cheeky.
incisive: Incisor: the tooth that cuts. An incisive comment slices to the point.
Scalpel analysis: the incisive analyst cuts away what isn’t relevant.
inexorable: In + exorare (to persuade by prayer): you can’t beg it to stop. Like the tide.
An inexorable rise of sea level: nothing pleads it away.
lambast: Same as lambaste: lam (beat) + baste (beat). A blistering review.
Think of a lamb being basted… with criticism! Lambast the movie harshly.
mawkish: Maggot in origin (mawk): sentimentality so sweet it makes you sick. A soppy greeting card.
Mièvre: syrup on top of syrup. Mawkish = sickly sweet.
meticulous: Metus = fear: afraid of errors, so careful. The accountant who checks every cell twice.
mitigate: Mitis = mild: to make milder. A lawyer’s mitigating factors soften the sentence.
Mitigate: like a mitten on a cold hand, it softens the sting.
obscure: Obscurus = dark. An obscure poet: you can’t see him because he’s in the dark.
Ob + scure: covered over. Obscure instructions hide their meaning.
perfidy: Per (through) + fides (faith): faith broken. La perfide Albion.
Perfidy = Judas’s kiss: a treacherous betrayal by one who seemed loyal.
platitude: Plat = flat: a flat remark with no depth. “Everything happens for a reason.”
Platitude: a cliché, said with a straight face: “Time heals all wounds.”
preclude: Pre + claudere (to close): close the door beforehand. A broken leg precludes running the marathon.
Preclude = exclude in advance. A fire precludes the use of the stairs.
predilection: Pre + diligere (to love): a prior love. A predilection for chocolate.
Prédilection: your favourite, chosen before the others. A weakness for something.
prescience: Pre + science: knowing in advance. The prescient trader sold before the crash.
Prescient sounds like “precious sight”: foreseeing the future.
querulous: Querela = complaint (querelle). The querulous guest sends back the soup twice.
Sounds like “quarrel-ous”: always whining over small things.
recondite: Re + condere (to hide): hidden away. A recondite theory only experts know.
Recondite = « abscons »: like a manuscript in a locked cellar.
reticent: Re + tacere (to be silent): holding back. A reticent witness says little.
Un homme réservé: reticent = unwilling to speak, not necessarily reluctant to act.
rustic: Rus = countryside. A rustic cabin: simple, wood, no frills.
Rustic charm: rough stone walls and a farm table. Rural simplicity.
superfluous: Super + fluere (flow over): the water running over the rim is surplus. Unnecessary.
Superfluous adjectives: delete them; the sentence works without them.
torpor: Torpedo fish (the electric ray) stuns you into numbness. Torpor = sluggish stillness.
Torpeur d’été: the heat makes you slow, like a lizard on a rock.
vociferous: Voc = voice + ferre (carry): carries a loud voice. A vociferous protest.
Vociferous: a crowd shouting complaints through megaphones.
volubility: Volvere (roll): words keep rolling out. A voluble talker never stops.
Volubilité: a taxi driver who talks nonstop all the way from the airport.
